articles.title: I went without a car for a month. How much money did I save?
articles.summary: With gas prices on the rise, the idea of saving money while having a spot of fun was wonderful – so I busted out my ebike for an experiment. This is the best electric bicycle I have ever tested. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: I ’m an avid ebiker, especially when the weather allows. During the summer, I drive my car close to 30% less than any other season. I have a few ebikes at home and they all go at least 20mph, so I can get around pretty quickly when I need to. There’s just something about hopping onto a bike instead of climbing into a car. There’s a certain freedom to it – probably similar to riding a motorocycle, but without the extra license, testing and insurance. Also without the speed, but you take the good with the bad.

Also, gas prices are insane these days, so any time I can spend not behind the wheel is a gift. Riding an ebike is a fun diversion from how I usually get around, but I wondered if I could actually do it for a full month and save a little money.

For one month, I rode an ebike or escooter exclusively (with a few notable exceptions we’ll discuss later) and tracked where I went and how far, and used Google Maps to track how long it would have taken to drive. I learned a few lessons along the way – a lot of big pros and cons – from safety to that extra bit of mobility.

articles.title: What is my cat saying? I asked experts to translate
articles.summary: Slow blinking and trilling are some of the ways felines show affection – but experts say to ‘read the whole cat in context’ I talk to my cat, Blue, constantly. I say things like, “You’re my little baby,” and “Wow, good jump,” and “Can you stop being a jerk for like, two seconds?” She also seems to…
body: She also seems to say a lot, like, “Feed me,” “Feed me right now,” and “Stop working and play with me.”
Because I’m obsessed with her, I like to think we have a perfect, mind-meld level of communication. But what if I’m wrong? What is Blue really trying to tell me? And what am I really telling her?
I turned to cat experts to find out how cats communicate, and how we can better understand them.
First, it’s worth exploring how cats perceive us, as this can shape how they communicate with us. Do they see humans as big, weird, hairless cats? Food dispensers? Or something else?

body: Our editors and writers have lived across the globe, from Abu Dhabi to Toronto to São Paulo. So when we asked them to share beloved gifts from outside the US, the answers were as varied as our home towns.

This is the stuff we bring home in our suitcases and press into friends’ hands. Take the “workhorse” German paring knives or the bright red tortilla press that makes homemade masa feel effortless. There’s a 3lb tub of Maldon salt that is absurdly whimsical yet practical, and a set of Australian linen sheets that get softer with every wash.

Some picks, such as El Dorado rum from Guyana, are a little piece of home. Others, including posters from Denmark’s Louisiana Museum, are just beautiful. And all of them are delightful discoveries that don’t require a plane ticket to bring home.

articles.title: Grace Cacciato Wins the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy U.S. Regional Final
articles.summary: Ten chefs. Five hours in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. One ticket to Milan. Meet the competitors of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy U.S. Regional Final.
body: The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the U.S. Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024-25 U.S. winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, D.C. and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

Saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

articles.title: Popcorn at The Paris Theater and Cocktails at Bergdorf’s: Inside Netflix’s Avedon Screening and After-Party
articles.summary: Ahead of its official streaming release on November 11, Ron Howard’s Avedon premiered at The Paris Theater, Manhattan’s longest-running arthouse cinema.
body: Richard Avedon, the revered photographer whose work has helped shape the legacy of Vogue, had a choice way of introducing himself: “I can’t write, I can’t type, I can’t read my own handwriting, but I can see like a son of a b*tch.” These are the very words uttered by the late lensman as he introduces himself in a new Netflix documentary chronicling his life.

Greatly influenced by film and dance, Avedon’s genre-defining artistic direction saw him remove models from the confines of studio backdrops and instead photograph them in everyday settings. “He was smart and he was also the right talent and individual for the right time, as it relates to the mediums of photography and magazines,” shared Howard while discussing the project with The New Yorker’s Adam Gopnik on stage.

articles.title: Gina Bruno Wants You to Be a Guest at Your Own Party
articles.summary: The private chef and food show host chats about her hosting philosophy and the essentials she turns to time and time again.
body: “Dinner is never just dinner. It is so much about the people, and the food is just the excuse to get those people around the table.”

I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes. The self-proclaimed “chef, mom, and host” wears a lot of hats. Private chef, event producer, event space owner, and food show host are just a few of the titles Bruno claims, but central to all of her work is a palpable love of people, and of creating a space for gathering, both of which make her a natural-born host.

Not everyone has a natural inclination toward hosting, though, so to help them out I asked Bruno to run me through her tips for throwing a gathering, be it an intimate dinner or a rowdy holiday party.

articles.title: Korean Hair Vinegar Is the Secret to Glossy, Glass-Like Hair
articles.summary: Trying to get glass hair shine? Korean hair vinegar might be what your strands have needed this whole time. Experts explain the pH trick behind the shine, plus the formulas worth trying.
body: If we’re being honest, shiny glass hair takes quite a bit of work. There’s the salon gloss every few weeks, the shine serum before you leave the house, and the professional blowout that never looks quite as glamorous the next morning. So when a two-minute shower step started promising the same mirror-like finish, it was bound to take off.

Enter Korean hair vinegar, which has been all over TikTok lately, with videos of dull, frizzy hair turning smooth and shiny after a single wash. It might sound like something you’d put on a salad, but the idea has deep roots. “In Korea, vinegar has always been both food and medicine,” says Ellie Byun, OMD, a doctor of Korean medicine and licensed acupuncturist.

Still, vinegar isn’t exactly the first thing you’d reach for to fix your hair, and plenty of viral trends don’t exactly live up to the hype. So does this one? Below, experts break down what hair vinegar actually does, who should try it and who should skip it, plus a few of our favorite formulas.
points: Korean hair vinegar might be what your strands have needed this whole time.

articles.title: How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate
articles.summary: Fake onion sites impersonate trusted platforms to steal passwords and crypto. Here's how to verify an onion address using Tor Browser's built-in checks.
body: The dark web isn't just for illicit activities. In fact, many legitimate online platforms maintain a ".onion" domain on the dark web for privacy reasons, including media outlets like ProPublica and BBC News, social media sites like Facebook, and privacy-conscious communication platforms like Proton Mail and SecureDrop.

But this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious users. And given that onion links are long and jumbled, it’s easy for users to accidentally click on the wrong link and end up on a fake website instead of the real one. When the FBI seized 276 onion addresses during 2014's Operation Onymous, they found that 153 of them were phishing sites.

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.
